title: Linking & Navigation
summary: Use Next.js Link for moving between local pages in an application.

subtopics.title: Import Link
subtopics.explanation: Import `Link` from `next/link` and render it around readable link text. Next.js can prepare nearby pages and navigate between app routes without requesting a completely new document in many cases. It is like an indoor hallway that avoids leaving and re-entering the building. Links still need to work with a keyboard and have a visible focus indicator. In practice, keep an internal destination in the app route format so navigation stays within the site.

subtopics.title: Choose a route
subtopics.explanation: The `href` property names the destination, such as `/products`. It should match a real route in the app. A link is a promise that the destination exists, like a sign pointing to a room. Avoid `href="#"` as a placeholder because it jumps unexpectedly and does not communicate a real destination. Use a button when the action changes the current page without navigation. In practice, a missing local route should lead to a deliberate not-found experience, not an empty screen.

subtopics.title: Describe the destination
subtopics.explanation: Link text should tell people where they will go, even when read outside its paragraph. “Read the setup guide” is clearer than “click here.” This is like labeling a door with the room name instead of “go.” Clear names help screen-reader users scan a list of links and help everyone decide whether the destination matches their task. In practice, make the visible link label understandable when a screen reader lists links alone.

subtopics.title: External links
subtopics.explanation: Use a regular `<a>` element for an external website or a file download. The browser then applies familiar behavior, including opening a new tab when requested and showing the destination URL. External navigation is like leaving the building for another address. If a link opens a new tab, tell users when that behavior may surprise them. In practice, use an anchor for another domain even when both sites share a brand.

subtopics.title: Check navigation
subtopics.explanation: Test a route by clicking its link, refreshing the destination directly, and using browser Back and Forward. These checks catch pages that only work after navigating from the home page. It is like checking both the hallway and the building’s street entrance. Also confirm links work when JavaScript is slow or unavailable where practical. In practice, check the destination after deployment because base paths and rewrites can differ.

foundations.overview: A link takes someone from the page they are reading to another destination. In Next.js, the `Link` component handles navigation between pages in your app and can make that change feel faster. Think of it like an internal hallway in a building. A normal HTML anchor is still the right doorway to another website. Every destination should be clear and directly visitable.
foundations.whyItMatters: Links connect routes into a usable information path. Clear text and valid destinations support keyboard navigation, direct visits, and search discovery.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser sees a normal `<a>` for each `<Link>` (so it's crawlable and middle-clickable), but Next intercepts the click and, instead of a full GET + reload, swaps the changed React tree in place. Prefetched routes are already in memory, so the click feels immediate and the URL/history update via the History API.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A site nav uses `<Link>` with `usePathname` to highlight the active tab; a search box reads `useSearchParams().get('q')` and updates results by pushing a new query string; a login form calls `router.push('/dashboard')` (or `router.replace`) after a successful submit.
foundations.businessImpact: Instant, prefetched navigation reduces perceived latency and bounce, while real `<a>` tags keep links accessible and SEO-friendly — directly affecting engagement and discoverability.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A clear split between declarative links and imperative routing keeps navigation logic predictable and testable, and the URL-as-state pattern (search params) makes shareable, bookmarkable UI states easy to build.
foundations.performanceImpact: Automatic prefetching trades a little background bandwidth for near-zero click latency. Disabling prefetch on rarely-used links and using `scroll: false` thoughtfully keeps navigation both fast and smooth.
commonUseCases: Primary navigation and content links via <Link>
Programmatic redirects after form submit/login with router.push or router.replace
Highlighting the active nav item using usePathname
Reading and updating filters/search via useSearchParams + router.push

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should import useRouter from 'next/router' in the App Router.
commonMisconceptions.reality: That's the Pages Router API. In the App Router you import useRouter (and the other hooks) from 'next/navigation', and they only work in Client Components ('use client').

commonMisconceptions.myth: A plain <a href> is fine for internal links.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A raw <a> triggers a full page reload, losing client-side navigation, prefetching, and persistent layout state. Use <Link> for in-app navigation; reserve <a> for external URLs.

steps.name: Render
steps.detail: <Link href> renders a real <a> tag, so it's accessible, crawlable, and works with middle-click / open-in-new-tab.

steps.name: Prefetch
steps.detail: When the link scrolls into the viewport (in production), Next prefetches the destination route's RSC payload in the background.

steps.name: Click intercepted
steps.detail: On click, Next prevents the default full reload and starts a client-side navigation instead.

steps.name: Reconcile segments
steps.detail: Only the changed route segments are swapped; shared layouts stay mounted with their state, so the transition is partial and fast.

steps.name: URL + history
steps.detail: The URL and browser history update via the History API; usePathname/useSearchParams reflect the new URL.

steps.name: Scroll
steps.detail: By default Next scrolls to top (and restores scroll on back/forward); scroll={false} keeps the viewport in place.

interactiveExamples.explanation: This mirrors the real pattern: compare the current path to each link's href to mark the active one. Here we simulate usePathname with state so it runs in the browser; in Next you'd read it from usePathname().
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Clicking a link bolds it and updates the shown path — the active link is highlighted like a real nav.

codeLab.title: Build an active-aware nav
codeLab.instructions: Complete the `isActive` logic so the link matching the current path is marked active (bold + aria-current). Click links to change the simulated path, then Run.
codeLab.expectedOutput: The link for the current path renders bold with aria-current='page'.
hints: In Next you'd get the current path from usePathname(); here it's the `pathname` state.
For leaf links compare exactly (===); for a section link you might use pathname.startsWith(href).

The `href` property names the destination, such as `/products`.

Use a regular `<a>` element for an external website or a file download.
